prompt: Where does the object that implements `BookRepository` come from?
hint: Look in `target/` after a build: nothing there implements it.

choices.text: A source file a Maven plugin generates under `target/` during the build
choices.why: That is code generation, and nothing of the kind is written: the build compiles only the interface.

choices.text: A proxy Spring Data creates when the application starts
choices.why: Right. At startup Spring Data finds the interface and makes an object that implements it, sending inherited methods to `SimpleJpaRepository` and declared ones to queries it builds then.

choices.text: A class named `BookRepositoryImpl` that you write next to the interface
choices.why: The point of the interface is that you write no implementation. The bookshop has none and still runs.

choices.text: Hibernate, from the entity mapping, when the persistence unit is built
choices.why: Hibernate maps `Book` to a table, but it knows nothing about repository interfaces; those are Spring Data's.

prompt: A `Book` with id 7, loaded in an earlier transaction and changed since, is passed to `save`. What does `save` do with it?
hint: The id is not `null`.

choices.text: It calls `persist`, which inserts a second row with a new id
choices.why: `persist` is for an entity Spring Data considers new, which by default means a `null` id. This one has an id.

choices.text: It refuses the entity because it is detached
choices.why: A detached entity is exactly what `merge` exists for, and `save` calls it instead of refusing.

choices.text: It calls `merge`, copying the changes onto a managed copy that it returns
choices.why: Right. That is why the caller should use what `save` returns: the object passed in stays detached.

choices.text: It does nothing until somebody calls `flush` on the repository
choices.why: `flush` decides when SQL is sent, not whether the changes are taken. `save` merges the state immediately.

prompt: Which of these can code call on `AuthorRepository` as this lesson declares it, without adding anything to the interface? Choose all that apply.
hint: Inherited, or declared, or neither.

choices.text: `save(author)`
choices.why: Inherited from `CrudRepository`; lesson 10 wrote it by hand and now nobody does.

choices.text: `count()`
choices.why: Inherited from `CrudRepository`, and it becomes one `select count(*)`.

choices.text: `findAll(Pageable)`
choices.why: Inherited through `ListPagingAndSortingRepository`, which `JpaRepository` extends.

choices.text: `findByNameStartingWith(String prefix)`
choices.why: A valid derived query, but one that exists only once somebody declares it. Spring Data builds queries for the methods in the interface, not for every name it could parse.

prompt: Match each interface to what it adds to the ones it extends.
hint: `javap` printed two of them.

pairs.right: a List wherever the parent returns an Iterable
findAll with a Sort or a Pageable

prompt: Which line of the startup log says that Spring Data has found the repositories it will implement?
hint: It is printed before the database is reached.

choices.text: `HikariPool-1 - Start completed.`
choices.why: That is the connection pool opening its first connection to PostgreSQL, which happens after the scan.

choices.text: `Initialized JPA EntityManagerFactory for persistence unit 'default'`
choices.why: That is Hibernate ready to map entities. The repositories are Spring Data's, and they were found earlier.

choices.text: `Found 2 JPA repository interfaces.`
choices.why: Right: `AuthorRepository` and `BookRepository`, one proxy each.

choices.text: `Started BookshopApplication`
choices.why: That line says the whole application is up, repositories included, but it names none of them.

prompt: `CatalogueReport` used to log `books.list().size()` and now logs `books.count()`. What did the old line cost that the new one does not?
hint: Compare what each one asks the database for.

choices.text: Nothing: Hibernate turns `list().size()` into a `count(*)` on its own
choices.why: Hibernate cannot see the `size()` call on a list Java already has. It sent the full select first.

choices.text: Loading every book as an entity, and mapping each to a DTO, just to count them
choices.why: Right. `count()` is one `select count(*) from book`, and the rows never leave PostgreSQL.

choices.text: A transaction: `count()` runs without one
choices.why: Both run in a transaction. `BookService.count` is `@Transactional(readOnly = true)`, and the inherited `count` has one of its own besides.

choices.text: A second connection from the pool
choices.why: One connection serves the whole service call in both versions; the difference is in how much data crosses it.

prompt: In a derived query's method name, the subject (`find`, `count`, `exists`) ends at the first `___`.
hint: `findByIsbn`.

prompt: A client calls `/books/search?q=ma_`. How does `findByTitleContainingIgnoreCaseOrderByTitle` treat the underscore?
hint: Think of what `escape '\'` is doing in the SQL.

choices.text: As a wildcard, so "The Time Machine" matches through "Mac"
choices.why: In `like`, `_` is a wildcard for one character, which is exactly why Spring Data escapes it before wrapping the text in `%`.

choices.text: As a literal underscore: it is escaped first
choices.why: Right. The client's text is matched as text; only the `%` Spring Data adds on each side is a wildcard.

choices.text: It is removed, and the search runs for "ma"
choices.why: Nothing is removed from the argument. It is escaped and bound as a parameter.

choices.text: The request is refused with a 400 before any SQL runs
choices.why: An underscore is a legitimate character in a title, and the endpoint accepts any text.

prompt: Somebody adds `List<Book> findByAuthorNmae(String name);` to `BookRepository`. When is the mistake reported?
hint: The compiler sees an ordinary method.

choices.text: When `mvn -q package` compiles the interface and checks the names in it
choices.why: To the compiler the name is just a name; the build succeeds, as it did for `findByTitel`.

choices.text: At startup, with a `PropertyReferenceException`
choices.why: Right. Spring Data parses every derived name at startup and stops at a property `Book` does not have; here it would follow `author` and find no `nmae` on `Author`.

choices.text: On the first call, as a 500
choices.why: That is what a native query does, since nothing checks it early. A derived query never gets that far.

choices.text: Never: the method returns an empty list
choices.why: Spring Data does not guess an empty result for a name it cannot read; it refuses to start.

prompt: The shop wants the books cheaper than a given number of cents, cheapest first. Which derived method name asks for that?
hint: Property, then keyword, then the order at the end.

choices.text: `findByPrice_centsLessThanOrderByPrice_centsAsc(int cents)`
choices.why: `price_cents` is the column. A derived query names the entity's field, `priceCents`, because it becomes JPQL first.

choices.text: `findByLessThanPriceCentsOrderByPriceCents(int cents)`
choices.why: The keyword follows the property it applies to: `PriceCentsLessThan`, not `LessThanPriceCents`.

choices.text: `findByPriceCentsLessThanOrderByPriceCentsAsc(int cents)`
choices.why: Right: the field, the comparison, and an `OrderBy` with its direction at the end.

choices.text: `findByPriceCentsOrderByPriceCentsAscLessThan(int cents)`
choices.why: `OrderBy` closes the name; a condition after it is read as part of the sort and the name is refused.

prompt: With the `@EntityGraph` removed from `findAllBy`, the first page held the seven books of five authors. How many SQL statements did that one request send?
hint: One for the books, then one per author, counted once each.

prompt: With the entity graph, the page query joins `author` with a plain `join`, not a `left join`. Why is that safe here?
hint: Look at the attributes of `@ManyToOne` on `Book.author`.

choices.text: `optional = false` says every book has an author, so requiring one loses no row
choices.why: Right, and the schema agrees: `author_id` is `NOT NULL`. With the default, `optional = true`, Hibernate would use a `left join` to keep books without an author.

choices.text: An entity graph always produces an inner join
choices.why: The join type follows the mapping. On an optional relationship the same graph produces a `left join`.

choices.text: Because `fetch = FetchType.LAZY` is set on the relationship
choices.why: `LAZY` decides when the author is loaded when nobody asks for it. It says nothing about whether a book can lack one.

choices.text: PostgreSQL rewrites `left join` to `join` when the result is paged
choices.why: Paging adds `offset` and `fetch first`; it does not change the kind of join Hibernate wrote.

prompt: A colleague proposes `fetch = FetchType.EAGER` on `Book.author` instead of the `@EntityGraph` annotations. What is the argument against it?
hint: Whose decision is it, and how many queries does it reach?

choices.text: JPA does not allow `EAGER` on a `@ManyToOne`, only on collections
choices.why: It allows it, and `EAGER` is in fact the JPA default for `@ManyToOne`; lesson 10's mapping chose `LAZY` on purpose.

choices.text: An `EAGER` author makes paging impossible
choices.why: Paging is about the books' rows; a `@ManyToOne` adds at most one author per row and leaves the page intact.

choices.text: It loads the author in every query, even where nothing reads it
choices.why: Right. `EAGER` is a decision about the entity, taken for every query; an entity graph is a decision about one query, where the author is actually read.

choices.text: It needs `spring.jpa.open-in-view=true`, or the author is never loaded
choices.why: Open-in-view matters for lazy loading outside a transaction. An eagerly loaded author is already there.

prompt: `GET /books/2` sends two statements: the book, then its author. Why does the lesson leave it that way?
hint: What grows with the data, and what does not?

choices.text: Because `findById` is inherited and cannot carry an entity graph
choices.why: It can: declaring `findById` again in the interface with `@EntityGraph` would do it. The lesson chooses not to.

choices.text: One extra statement for one book; N+1 is about lists
choices.why: Right. A single read with one lazy reference costs one more round trip, whatever the size of the catalogue.

choices.text: Because the second statement is served from the persistence context and is free
choices.why: It reached PostgreSQL: the second terminal showed it. The context only spares a load of something already in it.

choices.text: Because joining two tables is always slower than two selects
choices.why: For a list a join is much cheaper than one select per row, which is the whole N+1 lesson.

prompt: What does the JPQL in `@Query` name?
hint: `Book` and `priceCents`.

choices.text: The tables and columns, `book` and `price_cents`
choices.why: That is SQL, which `@Query` sends only with `nativeQuery = true`.

choices.text: The entity and its fields, `Book` and `priceCents`
choices.why: Right. Hibernate translates them to the table and columns when it writes the SQL.

choices.text: The getters of the DTO, `getTitle` and `getPriceCents`
choices.why: Those belong to the projection. The query names the entity; the aliases connect its results to the getters.

choices.text: The JSON properties the endpoint returns
choices.why: The JSON comes from the projection's getters, after the query has run.

prompt: Why does the query say `b.title as title, b.priceCents as priceCents`?
hint: `TitleAndPrice` has no implementation in the project.

choices.text: PostgreSQL needs an alias for every selected column
choices.why: It does not; the SQL Hibernate sent has no aliases on the columns at all.

choices.text: To rename the fields in the JSON
choices.why: The JSON property names come from the getters, which would be the same with any alias.

choices.text: So that Spring Data matches each value to a getter of `TitleAndPrice`
choices.why: Right: `getTitle` reads `title` and `getPriceCents` reads `priceCents` from each row.

choices.text: JPQL refuses a path such as `b.priceCents` in a select unless it has an alias
choices.why: JPQL accepts the path alone; the alias is for the projection, not for the parser.

prompt: After `findTitlesByAuthor("H. G. Wells")` returns, what has entered the persistence context?
hint: What did the statement select?

choices.text: The two `Book` entities, each with a lazy author
choices.why: No `Book` was loaded: the statement selected two columns, not entities.

choices.text: The `Author` named H. G. Wells, loaded by the join
choices.why: The join filters on the name and selects nothing from `author`; no entity comes out of it.

choices.text: Nothing
choices.why: Right. A projection reads values, so there is nothing to manage, no author placeholder and no N+1 to have.

choices.text: Two `TitleAndPrice` entities
choices.why: `TitleAndPrice` is an interface, not an entity; its proxies are not tracked by the persistence context.

prompt: Put in order what happens to `GET /books/by-author?name=H.%20G.%20Wells`.
hint: From the controller down to PostgreSQL and back up to JSON.
items: The proxy runs the query it prepared at startup, with the name bound
PostgreSQL returns the title and price of each book
Each row is wrapped in a TitleAndPrice proxy
Jackson writes the list as JSON
trap: The query was built and checked at startup, not when the request arrived.

prompt: With the catalogue sorted by title, which books does `?size=3&page=1&sort=title` return?
hint: Pages are counted from 0.

choices.text: The first three
choices.why: That is `page=0`.

choices.text: The fourth, fifth and sixth
choices.why: Right. Page 1 is the second page, so the query skips three rows and fetches three.

choices.text: Only the first: `page=1` asks for one page of one book
choices.why: `page` says which page, not how many; `size` says how many.

choices.text: The second, third and fourth
choices.why: That would be an offset of one row. A page boundary falls at a multiple of the size.

prompt: A client asks for `GET /books?size=5000`. What `size` does the page in the answer report?
hint: Spring Data has a ceiling, and the bookshop does not change it.

prompt: The first `GET /books`, with the default size of 20, sent one statement and no `count(*)`. Why no count?
hint: How many rows came back, against how many the page could hold?

choices.text: The count is only sent when the client asks for `totalElements`
choices.why: The client asks for nothing of the kind: the numbers are always in the answer, and here they came from arithmetic.

choices.text: The count was cached from the startup report's `count()`
choices.why: Nothing caches it; a later request for page 1 sent a fresh `count(*)`.

choices.text: Fewer rows came back than the size, giving the total
choices.why: Right. Spring Data does the arithmetic instead of asking: first page, seven rows, room for twenty.

choices.text: Page 0 never needs a count
choices.why: Page 0 with more rows than the size does need one: the total is unknown from a full page.

prompt: `GET /books?sort=price` answers 500 and the second terminal shows no SQL for it. What happened?
hint: `Book` has `priceCents`.

choices.text: PostgreSQL refused `order by price` because the column is `price_cents`
choices.why: The statement never reached PostgreSQL; the second terminal would have shown it.

choices.text: The sort text was pasted into the SQL and broke its syntax
choices.why: Sort parameters are never pasted in as text; that is exactly what keeps them from being an injection point.

choices.text: No property `price` on `Book`, and no handler maps the exception
choices.why: Right. The refusal is correct and the status is not: the mistake is the client's, and lesson 7's handler has no case for `PropertyReferenceException`.

choices.text: The page size went over the limit of 2000
choices.why: No size was given, so the default of 20 applied.

prompt: Which of these mistakes stop the bookshop from starting? Choose all that apply.
hint: Which strings does somebody read while the application starts?

choices.text: A derived method `findByTitel(String titel)`
choices.why: Spring Data parses every derived name at startup, and `titel` is no property of `Book`.

choices.text: An `@Query` that selects `b.price`
choices.why: Hibernate parses the JPQL against the entities at startup and finds no `price`.

choices.text: An `@Query(nativeQuery = true)` that selects a column `price`
choices.why: A native query is SQL that nothing checks against the entities, so its mistake waits for the first call.

choices.text: A client sending `?sort=price` to `/books`
choices.why: That arrives with a request, long after startup, and is refused then, with a 500.

prompt: Match each request to the SQL the second terminal showed for it.
hint: Look for what each one could not do without.

pairs.right: offset ? rows fetch first ? rows only, then a count
where b1_0.id=?, then the author by its id

prompt: A new endpoint lists the title and price of the books under a given price, cheapest first, twenty per page. Which repository method fits it best?
hint: A derived query, a projection and paging can be combined.

choices.text: `@EntityGraph(attributePaths = "author") List<Book> findAll()`, filtered and paged in the service
choices.why: It loads every book and every author to keep a few, and nothing it fetches is needed: the endpoint shows no author.

choices.text: `Page<TitleAndPrice> findByPriceCentsLessThan(int cents, Pageable pageable)`
choices.why: Right. The name gives the condition, the projection keeps it to two columns with no entity, and the `Pageable` brings the size and the sort by `priceCents`.

choices.text: `List<TitleAndPrice> findByPriceCentsLessThanOrderByPriceCents(int cents)`
choices.why: Right condition, right projection and right order, but no paging: every matching book comes back in one list.

choices.text: `@Query(nativeQuery = true)` with `limit 20` written in the SQL
choices.why: A fixed `limit` is one page with no way to ask for the next, and the query is no longer checked at startup.

prompt: Put in order what happens to `findByTitleContainingIgnoreCaseOrderByTitle`, from the application starting to the SQL reaching PostgreSQL.
hint: Some of it happens once, some of it on every call.
items: Spring Data finds BookRepository and makes its proxy
The name is split at By and Title is checked against Book
Containing, IgnoreCase and OrderByTitle become the query's condition and order
A call arrives and the text has its % and _ escaped
The escaped text is wrapped in % and bound to the query
Hibernate sends the select with upper(...) like upper(?)
trap: Escaping cannot happen at startup: the text only exists once a call brings it.
